introduction-when-an-incident-becomes-a-.core: Incidents are local failures, while disasters take out whole sites or regions (outages, ransomware, deleted accounts, natural events). Disaster recovery and business continuity plan for restoring the business when the normal infrastructure is gone.

first_principles.problem: A team that handles bugs well has no plan when an entire region or account disappears.
truths: Large-scale failures happen rarely but devastatingly.
Business priorities decide what to restore first.
derivation: Choose a **DR strategy** to match them.

analogy.title: A home fire vs. a regional flood
analogy.story: A kitchen fire is handled with an extinguisher; a regional flood needs an evacuation plan and a place to go.
analogy.breaks: DR is expensive, so not every system needs the highest tier.

check.q: What distinguishes a disaster from an incident?
check.a: A disaster takes out large-scale infrastructure (a site, region or account), requiring recovery elsewhere.

the-two-key-metrics-rto-and-rpo.core: RTO (recovery time objective) is how long the service can be down. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. Both are business decisions that drive architecture and cost.

first_principles.problem: Engineers build expensive DR without asking the business what's acceptable, or build none at all.
truths: Downtime and data loss have business costs.
derivation: Ask the **business**: how long can we be down? how much data can we lose?

analogy.title: Saving a document while you write
analogy.story: RPO is how often you save (minutes of work at risk); RTO is how fast you can reopen and continue after a crash.
analogy.breaks: Targets on paper mean nothing unless tested and achieved.

steps.detail: Spend DR money where it matters.

example.outcome: DR investment aligned with business needs.

check.q: Which metric does continuous replication primarily improve?
check.a: RPO, by reducing how much data could be lost.

dr-strategies-the-spectrum-of-cost-vs-sp.core: DR strategies trade cost for speed. Backup & restore is cheap (hours to days), pilot light keeps a minimal core running (tens of minutes to hours), warm standby keeps a scaled-down full copy (minutes), and active-active serves from several regions (near zero).

first_principles.problem: Teams either over-pay for active-active everywhere or rely on backups that take days to restore.
derivation: **Backup & restore**: lowest cost, RTO of hours to days.
**Pilot light**: data replicated, minimal infrastructure, scale on failover.
**Active-active**: full capacity in several regions, near zero.

analogy.title: Spare-tyre options
analogy.story: No spare (call a tow truck), a donut spare (limited), a full-size spare, or a car with run-flat tyres.
analogy.breaks: Faster tiers add complexity and new failure modes, such as split-brain.

example.title: Matching tiers to systems
example.outcome: the right DR strategy for each system.

check.a: Replicate data and keep minimal core infrastructure running, then scale up the rest on failover.

the-gold-standard-active-active-architec.core: Active-active serves live traffic from several regions at once, so losing one just shifts traffic. It achieves near-zero RTO and RPO but needs multi-region data replication, conflict handling, global routing and continuous capacity headroom.

first_principles.problem: For critical services even minutes of failover is unacceptable, and standby regions are often broken when they're needed.
truths: Regions running live traffic are continuously tested.
Data consistency across regions is hard.
Each region needs spare capacity to absorb another's load.
derivation: **Multi-region data**: global DBs (Spanner, DynamoDB Global Tables, CockroachDB) or partitioned ownership.

analogy.title: Two fully staffed restaurants on the same street
analogy.story: If one closes, diners simply walk to the other, which already has staff and stock.
analogy.breaks: It's complex and costly. Consistency trade-offs (CAP) can't be avoided.

check.q: Why is active-active DR considered 'always tested'?
check.a: Every region serves real traffic continuously, so failover paths are exercised all the time.

region-evacuation-and-failover-testing.core: A DR plan is only a theory until tested. Run regular failover drills (region evacuations, restore-from-backup tests, DNS cutovers) in production or production-like environments, and measure the actual RTO and RPO.

first_principles.problem: On the day of the disaster, backups turn out to be corrupt and failover scripts reference servers decommissioned last year.
derivation: **Restore backups** regularly and verify the data.
**Automate** failover and **fix** what the tests reveal.

analogy.title: Fire drills
analogy.story: You don't find out the exits are blocked during a real fire. Drills reveal it first.
analogy.breaks: Production drills carry risk, so start small and expand once you're confident.

check.q: Why must backups be restored during tests, not just taken?
check.a: A backup is only useful if it can be restored correctly; untested backups are often corrupt or incomplete.
